top.h1: What is Leonardo da Vinci's bridge?
answer: Two Leonardo designs carry the name: a bridge of poles woven to hold each other, in the
about 1485 to 1487, and a one-arch bridge over the Golden Horn in Istanbul, about 350 metres long, in
about 1502. Neither is known to have been built then.
top.answer_more: Both drawings, and the arch's sizes: in his hand. The year 1502: most scholars, from a dated note. His letter's year: disputed.

blocks.h: How does the self-supporting bridge of poles hold, and how is it built?
paras: By its own weight: each pole rests on another and carries a third, so the load presses the poles together and friction keeps them from sliding, with no nail, peg or rope, as the
explains.
Leonardo drew it on two sheets of the Codex Atlanticus, folios 69a recto and 71 verso, kept by the

in Milan and dated to about 1485 to 1487. They show a temporary wooden bridge for an army, and his note says to weave it. Whether his own version had rope is disputed: a museum in Vinci sees logs that stand without it, while

paras.text: a 2008 talk by the mathematician Hans Humenberger

paras: has them fastened with ropes. No record shows one built in his lifetime.

Classes build it today on a table, from sticks of one size. In this build the smallest bridge takes six sticks, two pairs and two cross sticks, and each further joint adds two cross and two long sticks, as Humenberger counts:

points: Two sticks lie flat on the table, side by side and a little apart: the first pair.
A cross stick lies across them, partway along.
A second pair, set closer together so that it fits between the first, rests one end on that cross stick and runs on between the first pair's sticks, under their far ends.
Those far ends are lifted, a second cross stick goes across the second pair beneath them, and they are set down on it.
The joint is locked: each pair carries a cross stick that carries the other pair, and weight presses them tighter.

Each further joint repeats steps 2 to 4, wide and narrow pairs in turn. With each joint the bridge bends further into an arch, its two ends on the table, and its end sticks stand steeper. When they stand so steep that they slip, the bridge has one joint too many.

pic.alt: A drawing in two parts. First, how Leonardo's bridge of poles holds, pairs of poles leaning on each other through cross poles, each cross pole lying on one pair and carrying the end of the next, with no nail or rope. Second, his bridge for the Golden Horn in Istanbul to one scale with other bridges: one arch about 235 metres across the water and about 41 metres high, about 350 metres long in all, beside the arches at Trezzo sull'Adda, 72 metres, and Verona, 48.7 metres, the footbridge at Ås in Norway, 40 metres, and today's Galata Bridge, 490 metres long.

blocks.h: Why was the bridge over the Golden Horn never built?
paras: Nobody knows: no answer from Sultan Bayezid II survives, as
note in a study of 2025.

Leonardo offered it to the Sultan in a letter that survives only as an Ottoman Turkish copy, probably a translation, in the Topkapı Palace archive in Istanbul. Found in 1951 and published in 1952, it is dated 3 July but gives no year: most scholars say 1502 or 1503, some earlier. In it he offers several works, among them this bridge and a second bridge.
A few years later, Condivi and Vasari tell, the Sultan asked Michelangelo for a bridge across the Golden Horn, and he did not go.

blocks.h: Would the bridge over the Golden Horn have stood?
paras: Most likely, if built as an arch of stone: in 2019 engineers at MIT built

paras.text: a model of it at 1 to 500

paras: from loose blocks, and it stood without mortar.
His note, in

: "The bridge of Pera at Constantinople, 40 braccia wide, 70 braccia high above the water, 600 braccia long", that is "400 over the sea and 200 on the land, thus making its own abutments". With the Florentine braccio of 58.3 centimetres, that is about 350 metres long, 235 of them over the water, and 41 metres high, enough, his letter promises, for a ship with its sail set. The longest arch before it, at Trezzo sull'Adda, spanned 72 metres. Where builders of the time would have needed ten or more piers, MIT notes, Leonardo drew one flattened arch, its ends spreading outward like a swallowtail against sideways sway.

The MIT team, Karly Bast and Michelle Xie with their professor John Ochsendorf, 3D-printed 126 blocks, set them on scaffolding, then took the scaffolding away: the model carried itself. When one support was moved away from the other, as weak ground might, it only deformed slightly until stretched to collapse. Leonardo meant to build without scaffolding, Orlandi and Giannantonio point out, and the model did not test wind or stone at full size.

Leonardo's note names no material, and MIT's report says his letter gives none either, though Bast's thesis calls his plan "a masonry bridge". MIT concluded that only stone could carry such a span. Other readings put a timber arch on stone piers, among them the Swiss engineer Fritz Stüssi's, who judged the bridge buildable in 1953, Orlandi and Giannantonio report. A year earlier the art historian Ludwig Heydenreich had called it pure utopia. The material is still disputed.

blocks.h: Has Leonardo's bridge been built in real life?
paras: Not at full size: no bridge after his sketch crosses the Golden Horn, but a smaller one has crossed the E18 road at Ås in Norway since 2001, and bridges of poles go up in classrooms.
The painter Vebjørn Sand pushed for the Ås bridge, and Norway's Public Roads Administration built it, the
and
record: about 100 metres long, its main span 40 metres, of glued timber. On the Golden Horn itself stands today's
, 490 metres long, the fifth on its site since 1845.

blocks.answer: From Leonardo's sheets, a copy of his letter, and tests made in our time.
known: The arch is on folio 66 recto of Manuscript L, a pocket notebook about 10 by 7 centimetres in the Bibliothèque de l'Institut de France. In the notebook the page stands upside down. The back of the leaf carries a note dated 6 September 1502, which is why most scholars date the sketch to that year. Ravaisson-Mollien printed the notebook
blocks.open: What stays open: the year of the letter, the material Leonardo meant, which braccio he used, and where exactly the bridge would have crossed.

subs.h: "The Golden Horn bridge was 240 metres long, with a span of 280."
paras: About 240 metres is roughly the part over the water, and 280 is MIT's figure. His note gives 600 braccia in all, about 350 metres.

subs.h: "The Sultan turned it down as impossible."
paras: No answer from the Sultan survives, so nobody knows why it was not built. Some scholars read the silence as a no.

subs.h: "The bridge of poles was made for Cesare Borgia in 1502."
paras: Its sheets date to about 1485 to 1487. The often read 1478 to 1518 is the span of the whole Codex Atlanticus.

blocks.h: See the machines in the museum
blocks.p: The museum has not built either bridge. The machines it has rebuilt in code stand in the Leonardo wing, in its mechanism hall, its court and its house, each labelled as a reconstruction, and this door opens the wing at its beginning.
